short: The absolutist who rebuilt Swedish finances and the army his son would spend.
full:
Charles XI was four when his father died in 1660, and a regency of high nobles governed for twelve years. Their foreign policy produced the defeat at Fehrbellin in 1675 and a Danish invasion of Skåne. The king, taking personal command at twenty-one, fought the Danes to a standstill at Lund in December 1676 in one of the bloodiest battles ever fought in Scandinavia, and recovered the province.

The war convinced him that the nobility had ruined the state, and the Riksdag agreed. The Great Reduction resumed alienated crown estates on a large scale, raising royal landholding from a small fraction of the country to roughly a third, and in 1680 and 1682 the Estates conceded him the power to legislate without them. He spent the money on the indelningsverket, an allotment system under which groups of farms maintained a named soldier and his cottage in peacetime. He fought no further wars, and died of stomach cancer in April 1697 leaving a solvent treasury and a standing army.
